headline: No public sign that Russia is preparing a conventional attack on the Baltic states. Hybrid pressure (sabotage, GPS jamming, drones and border provocations) remains high and active.
conventional_note: Nothing reported on troop massing, field hospitals or blood supplies moving toward Baltic borders. Estonia's intelligence service sees no intention to attack NATO this year; Danish and US intelligence see a low but growing risk of a limited test.
hybrid_note: Sabotage arrests in Germany, Poland and Romania this week, persistent GPS jamming around Kaliningrad, and armed escorts pushing migrants at the Latvia–Belarus border earlier this month.
changed: First edition, so there is no previous day to compare against. From tomorrow this section lists only what is new, rising or easing.
bottom_line: The gap between alarm and evidence is today's main story. The most-shared item, Reuters' report that the Pentagon asked the Baltic states to tone down their warnings about Russia, rests on four anonymous sources; dozens of outlets repeating it add reach, not corroboration. Meanwhile the physical signs that would come before a conventional attack are absent from public reporting. The realistic near-term risk is a deniable, limited incident (a drone, sabotage, a border provocation) rather than an invasion. Danish intelligence warned that Russia might blame weapons landing on NATO soil on Ukrainian jamming, which is worth keeping in mind when reading drone stories like the one in Lithuania on 18 October.

headline: Estonia refuses on the record to soften its warnings after the Pentagon report, and Lithuanian police tie Starlink arson attempts in three EU countries to one network. Still no public sign of preparations for a conventional attack.
conventional_note: No reports of troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains moving toward Baltic borders. Putin said on 29 October that Russia is ready for but does not want a war with Europe. The overnight blackout in Kaliningrad has an official technical explanation and no sign of military activity.
hybrid_note: Lithuania announced terrorism suspicions against two men linked to Starlink arson attempts in Lithuania, Bulgaria and Poland; Poland blames Russian intelligence. GPS jamming remains persistent. No new drone or border incident reported.
changed: No change in indicator ratings, so the threat score is unchanged. Incident counts: one sabotage case (the Starlink arson network, announced 27–29 October and not covered in yesterday's edition), zero in the other four metrics. New: Estonia's prime minister publicly rejected calls to tone down criticism of Russia, Peskov called Baltic rhetoric hysterically aggressive, Politico reported US pressure on Lithuania to let Belarusian potash through Klaipėda, and Kaliningrad had a region-wide blackout overnight.
bottom_line: The evidence still points to hybrid pressure, not preparation for invasion. The Starlink case is the most substantial new development: prosecutors in three countries have linked the attacks, and the Russian connection rests on a Polish minister's attribution and on reports that a Turkish gang's leader lives under Russian protection, while Lithuanian police say the motive is not yet established. The Pentagon story has moved from anonymous sourcing to on-the-record Baltic reactions, but those reactions disagree: Estonia's foreign minister says there was no official request, while its prime minister says allies are asking Estonia to hold back. Read together with the Politico potash report, the picture is US pressure on Baltic positions as part of a push for a deal with Moscow; both reports rely on anonymous European officials. The Kaliningrad blackout drew online speculation about sabotage, but nothing so far contradicts the authorities' explanation of a protection system tripping at a power plant. The Telegraph's report that Moscow will demand a NATO pullback to 1997 lines rests on unnamed diplomatic sources and is not confirmed by any official.

headline: A quiet 24 hours with no new airspace, border or sabotage incidents. Lithuania's defence minister and Estonia's prime minister say no US request to tone down warnings reached them, while Estonia and Latvia move to give border guards wider powers against crossings they say Minsk organises.
conventional_note: Still no reports of troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains moving toward Baltic borders. ISW reports nothing significant on Russian military activity in Belarus. The only new exercise news is the concept for Union Shield 2027, a Russia–Belarus drill set for next year.
hybrid_note: No new drone, sabotage or border incident in the last day, but the pattern of recent weeks (the Starlink arson network, persistent GPS jamming, Belarus-organised migration) is unchanged. Poland charged a Russian national with spying after he was caught photographing railway infrastructure.
changed: No change in indicator ratings, so the threat score is unchanged. Incident counts: zero in all five metrics (yesterday one sabotage case). New: Lithuania's defence minister and Estonia's prime minister both said no US request to soften their language reached them, so the claim tracker moves the Pentagon story from Likely to Contested. Estonia's and Latvia's interior ministers proposed closing crossing points with Belarus for a while and widening border guards' powers to use force. Correction: yesterday's edition said Lithuania had not commented on the Pentagon report; its defence minister had said on 30 October that he had no information about such a request.
bottom_line: The evidence picture has not moved: hybrid pressure continues, and there is no public sign of preparation for a conventional attack. The Pentagon story now faces on-the-record statements from Lithuania and Estonia that no request reached them, but those statements deny only an official request, and Reuters described informal conversations, so the two accounts can both be true. The Estonian and Latvian moves on border force are a response to months of Belarus-organised crossings, not to a new incident, and closing crossings would be a political choice with costs for both sides. ISW says the Kremlin keeps demanding that NATO return to its 1997 footprint, but the primary statement behind that is not cited, so the Telegraph report of a formal demand in talks stays unconfirmed. Reports of men being seized off Russian streets to sign army contracts point to recruitment strain for the Ukraine war rather than a build-up aimed at the Baltics. A quiet day in public reporting is not proof of a quiet day on the ground, especially for the logistics and medical indicators.

headline: An unidentified object, probably a drone, entered eastern Latvia from the Russia–Belarus border area on Sunday evening and left after about 30 minutes; its origin is unknown. No other new incidents, and still no public sign of preparations for a conventional attack.
conventional_note: No reports of troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains moving toward Baltic borders. NATO's top commander said on 30 October that conflict with Russia is not inevitable. This matches Lithuania's 2026 National Threat Assessment, which judges the near-term conventional threat low because Russia's forces are tied up in Ukraine.
hybrid_note: A new airspace incursion over Krāslava and Ludza in Latvia adds to a pattern of drones, sabotage, persistent GPS jamming and Belarus-organised migration. No new sabotage, jamming or border incident was first reported in the last day.
changed: No change in indicator ratings, so the threat score is unchanged. The airspace indicator stays Elevated but its trend moves from Unchanged to Rising. Incident counts: one airspace incident (the object over eastern Latvia on 1 November; yesterday zero), zero in the other four metrics, as yesterday. Also new to the tracker: satellite imagery of a large over-the-horizon radar under construction near Gvardeysk in Kaliningrad, first reported on 21 October.
bottom_line: Today's evidence is consistent with the Lithuanian baseline: a low near-term conventional threat and persistent hybrid pressure, with nothing suggesting Russian forces are being freed from Ukraine or redirected toward the Baltic direction. The Latvian incursion is the only new incident, and the facts are thin: the armed forces have not said what the object was or where it came from. Past stray drones over Latvia have included both Ukrainian drones pushed off course, reportedly by Russian jamming, and Russian ones, so neither origin should be assumed; Izvestia's headline calls it a drone and links it to stories about Ukrainian drones, which runs ahead of the Latvian statement. The Kaliningrad radar, seen on commercial satellite imagery, fits the baseline's picture of Russia steadily building long-term military capacity, but it is a sensor, not a sign of imminent action, and it is not known to be operational. The debate in Estonia over whether its warnings about Russia have become too predictable is a political argument, not new evidence about Russian intentions. Quiet logistics and medical indicators reflect a lack of public reporting, not proof that nothing is happening.

headline: Poland puts police on full readiness along the Kaliningrad border after intelligence warnings of possible Russian sabotage in the coming days. No new incidents were reported, and there is still no public sign of preparations for a conventional attack.
conventional_note: No reports of Russian troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains moving toward Baltic borders. Poland's operation is a police response to a sabotage warning, not to troop movements. This matches Lithuania's 2026 National Threat Assessment, which judges the near-term conventional threat low because most Russian forces are tied up in Ukraine.
hybrid_note: Polish police and counter-terrorism units have reinforced the Kaliningrad border area from 2 to 8 November after warnings from military intelligence and allied services. Estonia deported a Russian citizen its security service links to Russian intelligence. GPS jamming, drones and Belarus-organised migration remain the background.
changed: No change in indicator ratings, so the threat score is unchanged. The sabotage indicator stays High but its trend moves from Unchanged to Rising because of Poland's official sabotage alert; the airspace trend eases back from Rising to Unchanged as no new incursion was reported. Incident counts: zero in all five metrics (yesterday one airspace incident, the object over eastern Latvia). New: Poland's border operation and Estonia's deportation of a Russian citizen over intelligence contacts.
bottom_line: Today's evidence is consistent with the Lithuanian baseline: a low near-term conventional threat and active hybrid pressure, with no sign that Russian forces are being freed from Ukraine or moved toward the Baltic direction. The most important new item is Poland's operation on the Kaliningrad border, which the national police chief confirmed on the record and tied to sabotage and the actions of eastern intelligence services. The more dramatic detail, that armed groups might try to cross from Kaliningrad, comes from anonymous sources quoted by the Polish broadcaster RMF and has not been confirmed by any named official; several outlets repeating RMF count as one source. A preventive alert is not evidence that an attack is coming, and authorities have reported no incident so far. Estonia's deportation fits the baseline's warnings about hostile intelligence activity, but the evidence behind it is not public. Quiet logistics and medical indicators reflect a lack of public reporting, not proof that nothing is happening.

headline: Poland says it headed off a possible provocation on the Kaliningrad border, and Latvia now judges that one of two drones that entered its airspace was a Russian Geran. Neither event points to preparations for a conventional attack.
conventional_note: Still no reports of Russian troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains heading toward Baltic borders, and Lithuania's defence ministry has said its military intelligence sees no significant change in Kaliningrad. This matches Lithuania's 2026 National Threat Assessment, which judges the near-term conventional threat low because most Russian forces are tied up in Ukraine.
hybrid_note: Polish border guards saw people with flashlights near the Kaliningrad border shortly after midnight on 3 November, during an operation launched on intelligence warnings of sabotage and possible armed incursions. Latvia says a drone on 1 November was most likely a Russian Geran and a second on 3 November looked Ukrainian. GPS jamming and Belarus-organised migration remain the background.
changed: No change in indicator ratings, so the threat score is unchanged. Trends: airspace moves from Unchanged to Rising (a new drone on 3 November and Latvia's attribution of the 1 November drone to Russia); border pressure moves from Unchanged to Rising (the Sępopol incident); sabotage goes back from Rising to Unchanged because no new warning or case was added. Incident counts: 1 airspace incident and 1 border incident (yesterday all zero); sabotage, GPS jamming and official threats stay at zero. New: Tusk's on-the-record account of the warnings, Germany's brigade in Lithuania stepping up electronic surveillance, and Russia's embassy in Warsaw calling the sabotage warnings fake.
bottom_line: Today's evidence is consistent with the Lithuanian baseline: a low near-term conventional threat and active hybrid pressure, with no sign of Russian forces being freed from Ukraine or moved toward the Baltic direction. The Sępopol incident is real but thin: border guards saw people with flashlights on the Russian side, nobody crossed, and Tusk himself said he could not be sure a provocation was intended. The stronger part of Poland's case is the warnings behind the operation, which Tusk now describes on the record as coming from Polish, NATO and, according to AP, also Ukrainian and US services; their evidence remains unpublished, and Moscow dismisses them as fake without offering any counter-evidence. Latvia's assessment that the 1 November drone was most likely a Russian Geran matters more than the coverage suggests, because it reverses the stray-Ukrainian-drone framing pushed by Russian state media, but it rests on tracking data, not wreckage. Many headlines describe a 'thwarted provocation' as if an attack was stopped; the evidence supports only a quick response to suspicious movement. The planned US-brokered talks in Abu Dhabi on 10–11 November are worth watching against the baseline, since a ceasefire is the main development that could eventually free Russian forces. Quiet logistics and medical indicators reflect a lack of public reporting, not proof that nothing is happening.

headline: Poland's special-services coordinator warns that something 'very massive' could happen on both sides of the Kaliningrad border, staged to be blamed on Ukrainians, and Germany arrests a suspected organiser of the Starlink arson near Warsaw. There is still no sign of Russian forces preparing a conventional attack.
conventional_note: No reports of Russian troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains moving toward Baltic borders. A Lithuanian border-post commander describes the extra jet, helicopter and training-ground activity he sees as routine. This matches Lithuania's 2026 National Threat Assessment, which judges the near-term conventional threat low because most Russian forces are tied up in Ukraine.
hybrid_note: Poland's operation on the Kaliningrad border continues amid on-the-record warnings of sabotage or provocations in the first half of November; the minister coordinating Poland's special services says the warnings are serious but imprecise. German prosecutors arrested a man suspected of ordering the 23 September arson at a Starlink ground station south of Warsaw, which Poland blames on Russian intelligence. GPS jamming and Belarus-organised migration remain the background.
changed: No change in indicator ratings, so the threat score is unchanged. Trends: sabotage moves from Unchanged to Rising (a new arrest in the Starlink case and the Polish minister's warning of a large staged provocation); airspace and border pressure go back from Rising to Unchanged because no new drone or border incident was reported. Incident counts: 1 sabotage case (yesterday 0); airspace incidents and border incidents fall from 1 to 0; GPS jamming and official Russian threats stay at 0. New: the 'blame Ukrainians' warning from Poland's special-services coordinator, US European Command's force-protection campaign, and Lukashenko calling NATO an 'aggressive bloc' while insisting Minsk and Moscow will attack no one.
bottom_line: Today's evidence is consistent with the Lithuanian baseline: a low near-term conventional threat, with active hybrid pressure aimed at Poland and the Baltic states and no sign that Russian forces are being freed from Ukraine or moved toward the Baltic direction. The most important new element is Tomasz Siemoniak's on-the-record warning that a provocation could be staged to look Ukrainian; it fits a pattern the baseline describes (information operations and preparation for disruptive acts), but he himself called the intelligence imprecise, and no evidence has been published. The Starlink arrest is the strongest hard evidence of the day: prosecutors in Germany, Poland and Lithuania are building cases against a network that allegedly used hired criminals, though the link to Russian intelligence still rests on official allegations and press reporting rather than published proof. Russian state media present Poland's operation as a political distraction, but offer no evidence and ignore that NATO's top commander and several allied services shared the warnings. Coverage that treats the coming days, including Poland's Independence Day on 11 November, as a countdown to an attack goes beyond the evidence; heightened vigilance is justified, alarm is not. The Abu Dhabi talks on 10–11 November and the Pentagon's European troop options due around 6 November are the developments to watch against the baseline. Quiet logistics and medical indicators reflect a lack of public reporting, not proof that nothing is happening.

headline: Lithuania expels three Ukrainians it says were tasked by hostile intelligence services, and Poland charges six people over supplying Russia's military, as Russia's Security Council chief accuses Poland and the Baltic states of training people to undermine Russia. There is still no sign of Russian forces preparing a conventional attack.
conventional_note: No reports of Russian troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains moving toward Baltic borders, and no new Russian or Belarusian exercise announced near them. This matches Lithuania's 2026 National Threat Assessment, which judges the near-term conventional threat low because most Russian forces are tied up in Ukraine.
hybrid_note: Counter-intelligence activity is intense across the region: Lithuania's State Security Department (VSD) had three Ukrainian citizens expelled for paid filming and information-gathering tasks received over Telegram, Poland's ABW detained six people accused of supplying Russia with weapons components, and a Romanian court ordered the arrest of a man living in Russia over a 2024 sabotage plot. Poland's operation on the Kaliningrad border runs until at least 8 November, and a new OSINT map shows GPS interference along almost the whole eastern flank.
changed: No change in indicator ratings, so the threat score is unchanged. Trends: official Russian rhetoric moves from Unchanged to Rising (Shoigu's accusation that Poland and the Baltic states train people to work against Russia, and Zakharova's reminder that Russia may answer with 'asymmetrical' measures); sabotage moves from Rising back to Unchanged (activity continues at the same pace). Incident counts: GPS jamming reports rise from 0 to 1 (an OSINT map of interference on 3 November); sabotage cases stay at 1 (a Romanian arrest order); airspace incidents, border incidents and official Russian threats stay at 0. New: the VSD expulsions and the Polish ABW espionage arrests.
bottom_line: Today's evidence is consistent with the Lithuanian baseline: a low near-term conventional threat combined with active hybrid pressure, and nothing to suggest Russian forces are being freed from Ukraine or moved toward the Baltic direction. The strongest new facts are official ones: the VSD's expulsion of three people recruited online for paid reconnaissance-type tasks matches the baseline's warning about hostile services recruiting through messaging apps, and Poland's ABW arrests are backed by a court order. Both, however, rest on evidence that has not been made public, and the VSD did not say which country's services were involved, so 'Russia-linked' is an inference, not a published finding. Shoigu's claim that Poland and the Baltic states train people to destroy Russia from within offers no evidence and mirrors Western accusations back at the West; it is best read as narrative preparation, and possibly as justification for future 'asymmetrical' responses, rather than as a sign of military intent. Poland's warning window (the operation runs to at least 8 November, with Independence Day on 11 November) has so far passed without a confirmed incident, which neither proves the warnings wrong nor right. The Abu Dhabi talks on 10–11 November and any outcome of the Pentagon's Europe posture review, whose options were due around today, are the developments most likely to shift the baseline. Quiet logistics and medical indicators reflect a lack of public reporting, not proof that nothing is happening.

headline: A Finnish court jails a ship's captain and a senior officer over the New Year's Eve cable damage in the Gulf of Finland, Reuters reports Russian military satellites edging toward a second Finnish radar satellite, and NATO begins six weeks of German-led drills in Lithuania. There is still no sign of Russian forces preparing a conventional attack.
conventional_note: No reports of Russian troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains moving toward Baltic borders, and no new Russian or Belarusian exercise announced near them. This matches Lithuania's 2026 National Threat Assessment, which judges the near-term conventional threat low because most Russian forces are tied up in Ukraine.
hybrid_note: The Helsinki District Court convicted the captain and a senior officer of the cargo ship Fitburg of aggravated criminal damage for dragging an anchor across Finland–Estonia undersea cables, the kind of shadow-fleet incident the Lithuanian assessment warns about. Russian satellites keep shadowing commercial radar satellites run by Finland's ICEYE, which supplies imagery to Ukraine. Poland's operation on the Kaliningrad border runs until at least 8 November, and ACLED counts 20 suspected Russian hybrid events in Poland so far this year.
changed: No change in indicator ratings, so the threat score is unchanged. Trends: official Russian rhetoric moves from Rising back to Unchanged (no new senior statement against NATO or the Baltic states found since yesterday). Incident counts: sabotage cases stay at 1 (the Helsinki court's verdict in the Fitburg cable case); GPS jamming reports fall from 1 to 0; airspace incidents, border incidents and official Russian threats stay at 0. New: the Fitburg convictions, Reuters' report on Russian satellites approaching a second ICEYE satellite, and the start of German-led NATO drills with more than 6,000 troops in Lithuania.
bottom_line: Today's evidence is consistent with the Lithuanian baseline: a low near-term conventional threat, active hybrid pressure, and nothing to suggest Russian forces are being freed from Ukraine or moved toward the Baltic direction. The Fitburg verdict is the strongest new fact, because a court tested the evidence; but it found the crew guilty of criminal damage, not of acting for the Russian state, and a separate Finnish court dismissed charges in the Eagle S case in October, which shows how hard intent is to prove. The satellite story rests on public orbital data showing real and unusual manoeuvres, yet 'attack rehearsal' is one analyst's interpretation, Germany's space commander warns that capability is not proof of intent, and reported distances range from 26 metres to about a kilometre, so headlines run ahead of the evidence. US signals are mixed: Lithuania says two US battalions are heading to Pabradė while the Pentagon's Europe posture review is still pending and a Politico report, denied by Lithuania's foreign minister, says US officials raised Belarusian fertiliser transit through Klaipėda. Poland's warning window has so far passed without a confirmed incident. The Abu Dhabi talks on 10–11 November matter most for the baseline, since a ceasefire could in time free Russian forces. Quiet logistics and medical indicators reflect a lack of public reporting, not proof that nothing is happening.

headline: A gunman kills six people in Kraków's Main Square; Polish officials point to far-right views and have named no foreign link. Moscow says any Coalition of the Willing troops in Ukraine would be legitimate targets as the coalition's first drills open in Poland on 9 November. There is still no sign of Russian forces preparing a conventional attack.
conventional_note: No reports of Russian troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains moving toward Baltic borders, and no new Russian or Belarusian exercise announced near them. ISW reports manpower shortages in a Russian army in eastern Ukraine and no redeployments toward NATO territory, which fits Lithuania's 2026 National Threat Assessment: a low near-term conventional threat because most Russian forces are tied up in Ukraine.
hybrid_note: No new sabotage, drone or border incident was first reported in the last day, but the pattern the Lithuanian assessment describes (shadow-fleet cable damage, GPS interference around Kaliningrad, hostile-intelligence recruitment) is unchanged. The Kraków shooting is a likely target for false online claims; Polish officials have so far given no sign of Russian involvement. Poland's operation on the Kaliningrad border was scheduled to run until at least 8 November with no confirmed crossing attempt.
changed: No change in indicator ratings, so the threat score is unchanged (17 of 39). Incident counts: official Russian threats rise from 0 to 1 (Zakharova's statement that Coalition of the Willing troops in Ukraine would be legitimate targets); sabotage cases fall from 1 to 0; airspace incidents, GPS jamming reports and border incidents stay at 0. New: the Kraków shooting (not linked to Russia by officials), Moscow's reaction to the KOALICJA 26.2 drills in Poland, and ISW's reading of Russia's team for the 10–11 November Abu Dhabi talks.
bottom_line: Today's evidence is consistent with the Lithuanian baseline: a low near-term conventional threat, steady hybrid pressure, and nothing to suggest Russian forces are being freed from Ukraine or moved toward the Baltic direction; ISW in fact reports manpower strain on one Russian front. The Kraków shooting is the day's biggest news in the region, but so far it is a domestic crime: the interior minister cites the suspect's radical, possibly far-right views, police say he acted alone, and no official has named a foreign link, so any claim of a Russian hand runs ahead of the evidence. Zakharova's 'legitimate targets' line is a threat, but a repeat of a position Moscow stated in July, and it concerns troops in Ukraine rather than NATO territory; her claim that the KOALICJA drills aim at Russia's military defeat misrepresents an exercise built around deployment after hostilities end. Poland's Kaliningrad warning window reaches its scheduled end without a confirmed incident, which does not show the warnings were wrong. The Abu Dhabi talks on 10–11 November remain the main thing to watch for the baseline, since a ceasefire could in time free Russian forces. Quiet logistics and medical indicators reflect a lack of public reporting, not proof that nothing is happening.
